title: How to Fix "Low Resolution Images" Errors on Amazon KDP
description: Learn how to fix blurry, pixelated, or low-resolution image problems on Amazon KDP using correct DPI, Canva export settings, and print-quality best practices.

shortAnswer: A KDP low resolution image warning means at least one image does not contain enough real pixels for the physical size it will print. Fix it by finding the affected image, replacing screenshots or small assets with larger originals, keeping images near 300 DPI at final print size, and exporting the final file as PDF Print without extra compression.

faqs.question: What resolution does Amazon KDP require?
faqs.answer: Amazon KDP expects cover and manuscript images to be at least 300 DPI at their final printed size. That means the image needs enough actual pixels for the number of inches it occupies on the printed page or cover.

faqs.question: Is 72 DPI enough for KDP?
faqs.answer: No. A 72 DPI image is usually intended for screens, not print. It may look sharp in Canva or a browser, but it will often print blurry, soft, or pixelated when used in a KDP paperback or hardcover.

faqs.question: Why does my KDP cover look blurry?
faqs.answer: A KDP cover usually looks blurry because one or more source images were too small, stretched too large, exported with compression, or downloaded as screenshots or social media images. The fix is to replace the weak assets and export a print-quality PDF.

faqs.question: Why do screenshots fail on KDP?
faqs.answer: Screenshots fail on KDP because they capture screen pixels, not print-resolution artwork. Even high-density screenshots often become low DPI when stretched across several inches of a printed cover or manuscript page.

faqs.question: Can Canva export high-resolution KDP covers?
faqs.answer: Yes. Canva can export high-quality KDP covers if the canvas dimensions are correct, the placed images are large enough, and the final download uses PDF Print rather than a compressed standard PDF or JPG.

faqs.question: Can I upscale low-resolution images?
faqs.answer: You can upscale low-resolution images, but upscaling cannot fully recover detail that was never in the original file. Use upscaling only when you cannot find a larger original, then inspect the result carefully at print size.

faqs.question: Why does my proof copy look pixelated?
faqs.answer: A proof copy looks pixelated when the printed image was enlarged beyond its real pixel detail, compressed during export, or placed below 300 DPI at final size. KDP Previewer may not show every print artifact clearly, so the proof copy can reveal problems late.

faqs.question: How do I check DPI before uploading to KDP?
faqs.answer: Divide the image pixel width by the number of printed inches it occupies. For example, a 1800 pixel wide image printed 6 inches wide is 300 DPI. Also inspect the exported PDF at 200% zoom before uploading.

summary: KDP low resolution warnings are usually caused by screenshots, stretched small images, compressed exports, or source art that is below 300 DPI at the size it prints.
The most reliable fix is to replace weak images with larger originals, export from Canva or design software as PDF Print, and avoid resizing or recompressing the PDF after export.
Coloring books need special care because thin lines, grayscale washes, puzzle grids, and dark covers reveal resolution problems quickly in proof copies.
checklist: Each cover and manuscript image is close to 300 DPI at final print size.
No artwork was captured from screenshots.
No small JPG or PNG asset was enlarged to fill a large page or cover area.
Original image files were used instead of social media downloads.
Canva exports use PDF Print, not JPG or standard PDF.
The exported PDF was not resized, converted, or recompressed after download.
Text, logos, and line art remain sharp at 200% zoom in the final PDF.
AI images were generated or upscaled large enough for the printed dimensions.
Coloring book interiors have clean black lines and sufficient contrast.
A proof copy was reviewed before publishing the book live.

howTo.description: A practical workflow for finding and correcting blurry, pixelated, or low-DPI images before uploading a KDP cover or manuscript.

steps.name: Find the image KDP is warning about
steps.text: Open the cover or manuscript and identify every screenshot, stretched background, small illustration, AI image, or social media download that may be below print quality.

steps.name: Calculate effective DPI
steps.text: Divide the image pixel width by its printed width in inches. Repeat with height. Images used for print should be close to 300 DPI at their final size.

steps.name: Replace weak assets
steps.text: Use the original high-resolution file, a larger stock download, vector artwork, or a larger regenerated AI image instead of stretching a small file.

steps.name: Export as a print-quality PDF
steps.text: In Canva, use PDF Print. In professional design tools, use a high-quality print PDF preset and avoid aggressive JPEG compression.

steps.name: Inspect and validate before upload
steps.text: Open the exported PDF, zoom to 200%, check for blur or pixelation, then run the file through KDPPreflight before uploading to Amazon KDP.

content:
You finish a cover in Canva. It looks clean. The title is sharp, the background is crisp, and the thumbnail feels ready for launch. Then you upload the file to Amazon KDP and see a low resolution image warning.

That moment feels bigger than it usually is. Authors often panic because the design looked fine on screen, and a warning about low resolution sounds like the whole book may need to be rebuilt.

Good news: this is one of the most common KDP upload problems, and it is usually fixable without redesigning the entire book.

The problem is that screens hide print-quality issues. Canva, Preview, browser thumbnails, and even some PDF viewers smooth images so they look acceptable at normal viewing size. KDP printing is less forgiving. A paperback cover or illustrated manuscript needs enough real pixel detail to survive ink, paper texture, trim size, and physical viewing distance.

Most low resolution images KDP warnings come from five causes: low DPI, resized images, screenshots, compressed exports, and incorrect Canva export settings. Some also come from AI images generated too small, social media images downloaded after compression, or line art that looked fine as a thumbnail but falls apart in a proof copy.

This guide walks through exactly what "low resolution" means, how to find the weak image, how to fix it in Canva or professional design software, and how to prevent the same KDP image quality issue from coming back on your next upload.

## What You'll Learn

By the end, you will know how to:

- Understand the difference between pixels, DPI, and print size.
- Read a KDP low resolution warning without guessing.
- Check whether an image is large enough for a paperback cover or manuscript page.
- Fix a blurry KDP cover exported from Canva.
- Avoid screenshots, compressed downloads, and stretched graphics.
- Decide when upscaling helps and when it only hides the damage.
- Prepare coloring book covers and interiors with sharper line quality.
- Validate your exported PDF with [KDPPreflight](/tools/kdp-cover-checker) before uploading again.

## What "Low Resolution" Actually Means on KDP

Low resolution does not mean the file is ugly. It means the image does not contain enough real pixel data for the physical size where it will be printed.

A digital image is made of pixels. A printed book is measured in inches. DPI means dots per inch, and it describes how many image dots are available for each printed inch. KDP cares about the relationship between image pixels and printed size, not just how the image looks on your monitor.

Here is the beginner-friendly formula:

**DPI = image pixels divided by printed inches**

If an image is 900 pixels wide and you print it 3 inches wide, it prints at 300 DPI. That is good.

If the same 900 pixel image is stretched to 6 inches wide, it prints at 150 DPI. That is risky.

If it is stretched to 9 inches wide, it prints at 100 DPI. That will often look soft, blurry, or pixelated.

This is why thumbnails are misleading. A thumbnail uses a tiny display size, so a small image can look sharp. Print forces the same image to cover real physical inches. When there are not enough pixels, the printer has to spread the existing pixels apart or invent in-between detail. That is where blurry proof copies, fuzzy edges, and pixelated KDP print results come from.

Screens usually display around 72 to 96 pixels per inch. Modern phones and Retina displays can be denser, but design software still scales and smooths artwork for comfortable viewing. Print needs much more information. Amazon's paperback submission guidelines say all cover and manuscript images should be at least 300 DPI, and KDP's image formatting guidance uses the same 300 DPI benchmark for paperback and hardcover images: [Amazon KDP paperback submission guidelines](https://kdp.amazon.com/en_US/help/topic/G201857950) and [Amazon KDP image formatting guidance](https://kdp.amazon.com/en_US/help/topic/G202169030).

A practical example makes this clearer.

A 6 x 9 inch front cover at 300 DPI needs about 1800 x 2700 pixels for the front panel alone. A full paperback wrap needs even more because it includes the back cover, spine, and bleed. If you place a 1000 x 1500 pixel image across the full front cover, it may look attractive in Canva, but it only has about 167 DPI at 6 x 9 inches. KDP may warn about it, and the printed book may look soft.

The hidden issue is effective DPI. An image file can claim to be 300 DPI in its metadata, but if you enlarge it too much in your layout, the effective DPI drops. KDP is concerned with the image at the size it appears in the final PDF.

## Amazon KDP Image Resolution Requirements

For print books, KDP's practical resolution target is 300 DPI. That applies to covers and to manuscript images. Covers matter because they are inspected closely by customers, but interiors matter too, especially for coloring books, puzzle books, children's books, photography books, planners, journals with decorative pages, and activity books.

KDP's own help pages state that images should be at least 300 DPI, and that cover art should be high resolution. Amazon also recommends images be sized at 100% and flattened where appropriate before submission. That language matters because it means a file is not automatically safe just because the document was created in a design tool.

Think of print quality in three bands.

**Acceptable:** An image is around 300 DPI at the exact size it prints. Edges look clean, text stays readable, and fine detail is present. For a 6 inch wide printed area, the image should be about 1800 pixels wide or larger.

**Borderline:** An image is around 200 to 250 DPI at final size. It may pass upload, especially if it is a soft background, texture, or non-critical illustration. It can still look weak in a proof copy, especially on title text, faces, line art, or detailed patterns.

**Bad:** An image is below 150 DPI at final size. KDP may show a low quality images Amazon KDP warning, and the printed result is likely to look blurry or pixelated. Screenshots, small AI outputs, and stretched social media downloads commonly fall here.

Covers need extra care because they combine several risk factors: large physical size, full-bleed backgrounds, text overlays, barcode areas, and dark or high-contrast design elements. If your cover also has safe area or trim problems, fix those separately with the [safe area guide](/blog/how-to-check-safe-area-before-exporting-kdp-cover). If the cover looks blurry after upload but KDP does not show a specific low-resolution warning, the broader troubleshooting guide on [why your KDP cover looks blurry after upload](/blog/why-your-kdp-cover-looks-blurry-after-upload) is a useful companion.

Manuscripts with images are just as important. A coloring page made from a low-resolution image may produce rough, jagged lines. A puzzle grid exported from a screenshot may print with fuzzy boxes. A grayscale interior can lose subtle detail when a low-resolution image is converted for print.

## The Most Common Causes of Low Resolution Warnings

KDP low resolution warnings are usually not mysterious. They come from repeatable workflow mistakes.

### Using Screenshots

Screenshots are made for screens. They capture the pixels visible on your monitor, not the original artwork quality.

A screenshot of a logo, title treatment, worksheet, coloring page, or AI image may look fine at normal size. But when placed on a paperback cover or full manuscript page, it often becomes 72 to 144 effective DPI. Screenshots also bake in anti-aliasing, browser compression, and scaling artifacts.

The fix is simple: use the original source file. Use the original PNG, SVG, PDF, AI, PSD, or high-resolution JPG. If you only have a screenshot, treat it as a temporary reference and rebuild the element properly.

### Enlarging Small Images

This is the most common kdp dpi problem. A small image is placed into a design, then dragged larger until it fills the page or cover.

Dragging the corner handle does not add detail. It only makes each existing pixel cover more physical space. The image may still look smooth because Canva or your PDF viewer previews it with smoothing, but the printed proof can reveal the stretch immediately.

The fix is to find a larger original or reduce the print size of the image. Scaling down is safe. Scaling up is risky.

### Low-Quality Canva Assets

Canva contains many useful elements, but not every element is equally suitable for large print areas. Some graphics are vector-like and scale cleanly. Others are raster images optimized for digital graphics, worksheets, or social posts.

A tiny decorative sticker may work in a corner but fail if stretched across a full back cover. A low-quality cover image may look acceptable in the editor and then fail in KDP Previewer.

The fix is to avoid using small raster elements as major cover art. Use high-resolution uploads, vector elements, or larger premium assets that remain sharp at print size.

### Exporting as JPG Instead of PDF Print

JPG is lossy. Every JPG export can throw away detail to make the file smaller. That can create soft edges, blocky artifacts, and banding in dark areas.

For KDP print covers, export as PDF Print. Canva describes PDF Print as the option for printed copies, while PDF Standard is intended for lighter digital sharing: [Canva PDF converter guidance](https://www.canva.com/features/pdf-converter/). If you use Canva, this one setting often fixes the entire problem.

### Compressed Downloads

Images downloaded from websites, email attachments, messaging apps, or online marketplaces may already be compressed. The file size may be small because detail was removed.

The fix is to download the largest available original from the source. Avoid copying from a preview page. Avoid dragging images from a browser into Canva. Avoid using images that were saved through chat apps or social platforms.

### AI Images Generated Too Small

Many AI image tools default to 1024 x 1024 pixels or similar square outputs. That can be enough for a small decorative image, but it is not enough for a full 6 x 9 inch front cover at 300 DPI.

A 1024 pixel wide image printed 6 inches wide is about 171 DPI. Printed 8.5 inches wide, it is about 120 DPI. That is why AI art often creates an Amazon KDP blurry images problem even when the prompt result looked beautiful.

The fix is to generate at a larger size, use a reliable upscaler, or build the cover so the AI image does not occupy more physical space than its pixels can support.

### Downloading Social Media Images

Instagram, Facebook, Pinterest, and other platforms compress images for fast loading. Redownloading a design from social media gives you a degraded copy, not the original.

Never use a social media post as your print source. Go back to the original design file or original photo.

## How to Check Image Quality Before Uploading to KDP

You do not need to be a designer to check image quality. You need a repeatable workflow.

Start by identifying every raster image in your cover or manuscript. Raster images include JPG, PNG, TIFF, screenshots, scanned art, exported AI images, and photos. Vector text and vector shapes are usually less risky because they can scale cleanly.

Next, check dimensions. Find the image's pixel width and height. On macOS, use Get Info. On Windows, use Properties. In Photoshop or Affinity, use Image Size or document information. In Canva, select the image and look for obvious low-quality warnings, but do not rely only on Canva's on-screen appearance.

Then calculate effective DPI. If a background image is 2400 pixels wide and prints 8 inches wide, it is 300 DPI. If it prints 12 inches wide, it is 200 DPI. Do the same for height.

After that, inspect the export. Open the final PDF, not just the source design. Zoom to 200%. Check title text, line art, faces, cover backgrounds, borders, puzzle grids, and any image that fills a large part of the page.

A good image at high zoom will look detailed, even if zoomed beyond normal reading size. A bad image will show square pixels, fuzzy boundaries, smeared texture, or jagged lines.

For Canva, use this workflow:

1. Set the cover or page size correctly before designing.
2. Use original high-resolution uploads.
3. Avoid screenshots and social media downloads.
4. Download as PDF Print.
5. Open the PDF locally and inspect at 200% zoom.
6. Run the PDF through [KDPPreflight's cover checker](/tools/kdp-cover-checker) before uploading.

For Photoshop, use this workflow:

1. Create the document at the final print size and 300 DPI from the beginning.
2. Place images as smart objects when possible.
3. Check each placed image's effective resolution after scaling.
4. Keep text live or vector-based.
5. Export with a high-quality print PDF preset.
6. Avoid aggressive JPEG compression in the PDF settings.

For a free-tool workflow, use file properties plus a PDF viewer. Check the image pixel dimensions, divide by printed inches, open the exported PDF, and zoom deeply into problem areas. It is not as elegant as professional preflight software, but it catches many obvious failures.

## Canva Fix for Low Resolution KDP Covers

Canva can produce sharp KDP covers, but the setup has to be print-aware.

First, create the correct canvas size. Do not design only the front cover if KDP expects a full paperback wrap. A paperback cover file needs back cover, spine, front cover, and bleed. If your cover file dimensions are wrong, you may also run into mismatch errors. For that problem, use the guide on [interior and cover file mismatch on KDP](/blog/interior-and-cover-file-dont-match-kdp).

Second, use the right source images. If your front cover background is a photo, illustration, or AI image, it needs enough pixels for the final front panel. For a 6 x 9 inch front panel, aim for at least 1800 x 2700 pixels before bleed. More is safer if you crop heavily.

Third, avoid screenshots. Do not screenshot a Canva page, a generated image preview, a logo, or a worksheet and place that screenshot back into the cover. Use exported originals or vector files.

Fourth, avoid resizing after export. Do not download a PDF, upload it to another converter, resize it, compress it, convert it to JPG, and then convert it back to PDF. Each step increases the chance of quality loss or incorrect page dimensions.

Fifth, export correctly. In Canva, choose Share, Download, file type PDF Print. If you need bleed, enable bleed in the design and make sure backgrounds extend past the trim area. Canva's PDF options can vary by interface updates, so the practical rule is to choose the print-oriented PDF option and avoid standard PDF or JPG for KDP covers.

A common beginner mistake is trusting the canvas preview. Canva previews are optimized for editing speed. They are not a print proof. Always inspect the final PDF.

Another mistake is using a cover image downloaded from a template preview. Template previews are not the same as editable high-resolution assets. Work inside the original Canva design and export from there.

## Why Images Become Blurry After Resizing

Resizing is where many low quality images Amazon KDP problems begin.

When you enlarge a raster image, the software must create new pixels between the original pixels. This process is called interpolation. The tool guesses what the missing pixels should be based on nearby colors.

Interpolation can make an enlarged image smoother, but it cannot recover true detail that never existed. A small photo of a face does not gain real eyelashes when stretched. A low-resolution coloring page does not gain crisp line edges when enlarged. A 1024 pixel AI image does not become a true 300 DPI full cover just because the document says 300 DPI.

This is why "setting the DPI to 300" is not a magic fix. If you change the DPI metadata without adding real pixels, only the label changes. If you resample the image upward, the pixel count increases, but much of the added detail is guessed.

Print magnifies the problem. On screen, smoothing can hide the guessed pixels. On paper, ink and paper texture reveal soft transitions, jagged diagonals, and smeared details.

The safest rule is simple: start larger than you need. A large image can be reduced cleanly. A small image enlarged too far will always carry risk.

## How to Improve Low-Quality Images for KDP

The best fix is not always upscaling. The best fix is usually replacing the weak image.

First, look for the original. If the image came from a camera, stock site, illustrator, AI tool, or Canva upload, find the highest-resolution version. Do not use the version exported for social media or email.

Second, use vector graphics where possible. Logos, icons, borders, typography, puzzle grids, and line illustrations often work better as vector artwork than raster images. Vector shapes stay crisp at any size because they are defined mathematically rather than by fixed pixels.

Third, regenerate AI art larger if possible. If your AI image was created at 1024 x 1024 and you need a full front cover, regenerate at a larger size or use an AI workflow that supports high-resolution output. Avoid cropping so aggressively that the remaining image area becomes too small.

Fourth, upscale carefully. Upscaling can help when the original is close to acceptable, such as increasing a 240 DPI image toward 300 DPI. It is less reliable when trying to turn a tiny screenshot into a full cover background. After upscaling, inspect line edges, faces, text, and fine texture. If the result looks waxy, smeared, or over-sharpened, it may still print poorly.

Fifth, sharpen lightly. A small amount of sharpening can improve perceived crispness, especially after resizing. Too much sharpening creates halos and crunchy edges that look unprofessional in print.

Sixth, avoid excessive compression. Save working files in high-quality formats. Export the final KDP file once, from the source design, using print settings.

Be realistic about recovery. Some images are too damaged to rescue. If a screenshot is 600 pixels wide and must print across a full 8.5 inch page, rebuilding or replacing it will produce a better result than any filter.

## Best Image Practices for KDP Coloring Books

Coloring books are especially sensitive to resolution because the product depends on line quality. Readers need clean outlines, printable contrast, and enough detail for markers, colored pencils, and crayons.

Line art should be crisp. Thin gray lines that look elegant on screen may disappear or break up in print. For coloring pages, strong black lines usually work better than pale gray outlines. If the line art was generated by AI, inspect it carefully for fuzzy edges, broken contours, and accidental texture inside areas meant to be colored.

Black backgrounds need care. A black coloring book cover can look premium, but dark areas reveal compression artifacts quickly. If the black background is a compressed JPG, it may print with visible squares, bands, or uneven patches. Use solid fills, vectors, or high-quality images instead.

Grayscale interiors can be tricky. KDP printing may soften subtle tones, and low-resolution grayscale images can become muddy. Keep important details high contrast.

Thin puzzle lines and mosaic grids need enough pixel density. A maze, dot marker page, cryptogram, or mosaic image exported as a low-resolution screenshot can print with soft boxes and uneven borders. Use vector grids or high-resolution exports.

Cover-quality examples:

- A 300 DPI black-and-white mandala exported as PDF Print usually prints cleanly.
- A screenshot of a mandala from a browser preview often prints jagged or fuzzy.
- A vector title over a high-resolution illustration stays sharp.
- A rasterized title captured as an image can look soft even if the background is acceptable.

For color-sensitive covers, also read [KDP cover colors look different after printing](/blog/kdp-cover-colors-look-different-after-printing). Resolution and color are separate problems, but they often appear together in proof copies.

## Why KDP Preview Can Look Different from Final Print

KDP Previewer is useful, but it is not the same as holding a proof copy.

The browser scales the preview to fit your screen. That scaling can make some edges look softer or sharper than they will appear in print. Anti-aliasing smooths diagonal lines and text on screen. Preview compression can also simplify what you see, especially when zoomed out.

The final print depends on paper type, ink coverage, laminate, trim variation, and the original file quality. Matte covers can appear softer than glossy covers. Interior paper can make low-contrast grayscale art look flatter. Dark covers can show compression blocks or banding that were subtle on screen.

This cuts both ways. Sometimes KDP Previewer looks slightly blurry while the physical proof is acceptable. Other times the Previewer looks acceptable, but the proof copy reveals pixelation in large printed areas.

Use Previewer as a warning system, not the final authority. If the design contains important images, order a proof copy before publishing live. For layout preview and cover checks before upload, use [KDPPreflight's preview tools](/preview) and export validation tools to catch obvious issues earlier.

## Final KDP Resolution Checklist

Before uploading again, walk through this list:

- 300 DPI verified for important images at final print size.
- Original assets used instead of screenshots.
- No social media downloads used as print sources.
- No small raster image stretched across a large cover or page.
- Canva exported as PDF Print.
- Professional design tools exported with high-quality print PDF settings.
- No post-export resizing, conversion, or compression.
- Text remains sharp at 200% zoom in the final PDF.
- Line art and coloring book pages have clean contrast.
- Proof copy reviewed before the book is published live.

If you still see a warning, isolate the image. Replace the most suspicious asset first: screenshots, full-page backgrounds, AI images, and large decorative elements are usually the cause.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What resolution does Amazon KDP require?

Amazon KDP expects print images to be at least 300 DPI at final printed size. This applies to cover images and manuscript images. The important measurement is effective DPI after the image is placed and scaled in the final PDF.

### Is 72 DPI enough for KDP?

No. 72 DPI is screen resolution, not print resolution. A 72 DPI image may look sharp in a browser or Canva preview, but it usually prints blurry or pixelated when used in a paperback, hardcover, or image-heavy manuscript.

### Why does my KDP cover look blurry?

Your KDP cover is usually blurry because a source image was too small, stretched too large, compressed during export, or captured as a screenshot. Exporting as JPG or standard PDF can also soften the final cover.

### Why do screenshots fail on KDP?

Screenshots fail because they capture only the pixels visible on a screen. When stretched across printed inches, those pixels are not dense enough for 300 DPI print quality. Use original image files or vector artwork instead.

### Can Canva export high-resolution KDP covers?

Yes. Canva can export high-resolution KDP covers when the canvas size is correct, source assets are large enough, and the final download uses PDF Print. Canva cannot fix a low-resolution image that was imported into the design.

### Can I upscale low-resolution images?

You can upscale, but it is not a perfect fix. Upscaling can improve borderline images, but it cannot recreate detail that was missing from a tiny screenshot or heavily compressed JPG. Always inspect the upscaled result before upload.

### Why does my proof copy look pixelated?

A proof copy looks pixelated when printed images were below 300 DPI at final size, enlarged too far, or compressed before upload. Proof copies reveal physical print problems that screen previews can hide.

### How do I check DPI before uploading to KDP?

Check the image pixel dimensions and divide by the printed inches it occupies. A 1800 pixel wide image printed 6 inches wide is 300 DPI. Then inspect the exported PDF at 200% zoom and validate it before uploading.

## Fix the Warning Before You Upload Again

A KDP low resolution warning is not a verdict on your whole book. It is a signal that one or more images need better source quality, better sizing, or a cleaner export.

Start with the obvious suspects: screenshots, stretched images, compressed downloads, AI art that is too small, and Canva exports that used the wrong PDF setting. Replace or rebuild those assets, export as PDF Print, inspect the final PDF, and upload the corrected file.

Before sending the new file to Amazon, run it through [KDPPreflight](/tools/kdp-cover-checker). It gives you a faster way to catch low-resolution assets, export mistakes, cover sizing issues, and print-readiness problems before KDP or a proof copy catches them later.
